title: Boosting: AdaBoost & Gradient Boosting
html:
Boosting builds an ensemble sequentially: each new weak model concentrates on what the current ensemble gets wrong. It mainly reduces bias, and gradient-boosted trees (XGBoost, LightGBM, CatBoost, scikit-learn's HistGradientBoosting) are the go-to models for tabular data.

Bagging / random forestBoosting
TrainingParallel, independent modelsSequential, each depends on the previous ones
Base learnersDeep, low-bias treesShallow, high-bias trees (stumps to depth ~8)
Mainly reducesVarianceBias (and some variance)
Overfits when adding learners?NoYes — control with learning rate and early stopping
Sensitivity to noisy labelsRobustMore sensitive (keeps chasing hard/mislabelled points)

AdaBoost

AdaBoost (labels ±1) re-weights the training rows after each round: misclassified rows gain weight, so the next weak learner focuses on them. Each learner gets a vote proportional to its accuracy:

εₜ = weighted error of learner t αₜ = ½ · ln((1 − εₜ) / εₜ) wᵢ ← wᵢ · exp(−αₜ yᵢ hₜ(xᵢ)), then normalise F(x) = sign(Σₜ αₜ hₜ(x))

Gradient boosting

Fₘ(x) = Fₘ₋₁(x) + η · hₘ(x) hₘ is fitted to the negative gradient −∂L(y, F)/∂F at Fₘ₋₁

Start from a constant (the mean for squared error), then repeatedly fit a small regression tree to the pseudo-residuals and add a shrunken copy of it (learning rate η). For squared-error loss the negative gradient is exactly the residual y − F(x); for log-loss it is y − p. Other losses give other pseudo-residuals — that's what “gradient” boosting means.

Learning rate, number of trees and early stopping

A smaller learning rate needs more trees but usually generalises better. Too many trees overfit — so hold out validation data and stop when it stops improving:

The modern libraries

LibraryKey ideas
scikit-learn HistGradientBoosting*Bins features into ≤ 255 buckets for fast split finding (inspired by LightGBM); native missing-value and categorical support; built-in early stopping
XGBoostSecond-order (gradient + Hessian) updates; explicit regularisation of the tree (lambda, alpha on leaf weights, gamma per extra leaf); sparsity-aware splits; histogram method; GPU support
LightGBMHistogram-based; leaf-wise growth (control with num_leaves); gradient-based one-side sampling (GOSS) and exclusive feature bundling (EFB) for speed
CatBoostOrdered target statistics for categorical features and ordered boosting to avoid target leakage; symmetric (oblivious) trees; strong defaults
HyperparameterTypical rangeEffect
Learning rate (eta)0.01 – 0.3Smaller = more trees needed, usually better
Number of trees100s – 1000s (use early stopping)Too many overfits
Tree depth / num_leavesdepth 3–8 / 15–255 leavesInteraction order and capacity
Row / column subsampling0.5 – 1.0Adds randomness, reduces variance (stochastic gradient boosting)
min_child_weight / min_samples_leafProblem-dependentPrevents tiny, noisy leaves
L1/L2 on leaf weights0 – 10Regularisation
What is the difference between bagging and boosting?

Bagging trains models independently on bootstrap samples and averages them — it reduces variance and doesn't overfit as models are added. Boosting trains models sequentially, each correcting the current ensemble's errors — it reduces bias, is usually more accurate on tabular data, but can overfit and needs a learning rate and early stopping.

Why is it called gradient boosting?

Each new tree is fitted to the negative gradient of the loss with respect to the current predictions — gradient descent in function space. For squared error those are the ordinary residuals, but any differentiable loss (log-loss, Huber, quantile) works the same way.

Why do gradient-boosted trees often beat neural networks on tabular data?

Tabular features are heterogeneous, often uninformative, and relationships have sharp thresholds; trees handle mixed scales, missing values and irregular functions naturally and need less data and tuning. Neural networks shine when there is spatial/sequential structure (images, text) or very large datasets.
